We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for me to lie to my brother about having Asperger's syndrome for the rest of our lives. Let me break this down step by step. First, I know my brother has Asperger's, and he's been diagnosed. He's really smart, excels in math and physics, and is doing well in college. But he's been struggling emotionally, even to the point of attempting suicide. He's in outpatient treatment now. I'm his older brother, and we're super close. He only talks to me about these things. A few months ago, after his suicide attempt, I took him to the hospital. The nurse there mentioned that he might have autism because of some signs she noticed. I talked to him about it today, but he's still denying it. He's embarrassed about it, which I get, but I want him to accept it and not feel ashamed. I've tried telling him that people like Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs are thought to have Asperger's, but that doesn't seem to help. He still denies it. Now, I'm thinking about lying to him and telling him I have Asperger's too. My hope is that if he thinks I have it, he'll feel less alone and maybe stop denying his own diagnosis. I want to help him move forward in life. But is lying to him the right thing to do? I need to consider the moral implications. On one hand, lying could help him feel supported and less isolated, which is a good thing. It might encourage him to accept his diagnosis and seek help if needed. On the other hand, lying can break trust. If he finds out I lied, he might feel betrayed, which could damage our relationship. I also have to think about the potential consequences. If I lie about having Asperger's, would that be harmful in any way? Could it make him less likely to get the help he needs if he thinks he's not alone? Or could it prevent him from seeking treatment because he thinks he's just like me and I'm managing without issues? Another angle is the intention behind the lie. My intention is purely to help him feel better and encourage him to accept his diagnosis. But does the ends justify the means in this case? Is it acceptable to lie if it leads to a positive outcome? I also wonder about the long-term effects. If I lie for the rest of our lives, will that create more problems down the line? What if he starts to notice things that don't add up, or if other people find out? It could lead to more complications than I anticipate. I should also consider alternative approaches. Instead of lying, maybe there's another way to help him accept his diagnosis. Perhaps encouraging him to talk to a therapist or join a support group where he can meet others with Asperger's. Or maybe finding more relatable examples of successful people with Asperger's who he admires. But I'm not sure if those approaches would work as effectively as lying. He's been resistant so far, and maybe a lie is the only way to get through to him. I have to weigh the potential benefits against the risks of betrayal and broken trust. In the end, I'm torn. On one side, I want to help him as much as possible, and lying might achieve that. On the other side, lying could have serious negative consequences that I'm not fully anticipating. I need to decide whether the good intentions behind the lie outweigh the moral issues of deception.
